title: Given an N by N matrix where each row and each column is sorted in ascending order, find the Kth smallest element in the matrix. Explain the K-way Merge heap technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix (Row and Column Sorted Matrix)
keyPoints: Each row of the matrix is a sorted list, making this a K-way Merge over N rows.
The heap entry stores the value, the row, and the column to locate the next element.
Pop K times from the min-heap to find the Kth smallest element.
Only the row-sorted property is required for correctness; column-sorted is a bonus.
Time complexity is O(K log N) and space is O(N) for the heap.
An alternative binary search approach on the value range achieves O(N log(max-min)) time.

s1_definition.oneliner: Treat each row as a sorted list, run K-way Merge across rows, and stop at the Kth pop.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix** treats each row as a sorted list and applies early-stopped K-way Merge.
- A **min-heap** is seeded with the first element of each row, carrying `{value, row, col}`.
- We **pop K times**, pushing the next column element from the same row after each pop.
- The **Kth popped value** is the answer.
- Only the **row-sorted** property is needed; column-sorted is not required for this approach.
- Time is **O(K log N)** and space is **O(N)** for an N-by-N matrix.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps a grid of service fees where each row and column increases. To find the Kth cheapest fee for a pricing tier boundary, a clerk starts with the leftmost fee of every row on a tray, pops the cheapest, and slides one step right in that same row. After K pops, the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix is a K-way Merge problem once you notice that each row is already a sorted list. You seed a min-heap with the first element of each row, carrying the value along with its row and column so you can fetch the next element in that row. Then you pop K times, pushing the next cell to the right after each pop. The value of the Kth pop is the Kth smallest in the whole matrix.

The important point for interviewers is that only the row-sorted property is required for this approach to be correct. The column-sorted property is a nice bonus the problem provides, but the heap merge does not depend on it. The heap holds at most N candidates, so K pops cost O(K log N) time with O(N) space.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this on a fee grid where moving right or down only increased the fee. The product team needed the Kth smallest fee to set a pricing tier boundary. Rather than flattening and sorting all N^2 cells, Rajesh ran a row-wise K-way merge and stopped at the Kth removal, which was significantly faster for small K.

The senior-level insight is knowing both the heap approach and the binary search alternative, and understanding when each is better: the heap excels when K is small, while binary search excels when K approaches N^2. Being able to articulate which matrix property each approach uses demonstrates deep understanding.

Remember one sentence: treat rows as sorted lists, seed a heap with column zero of each row, and the Kth pop gives the Kth smallest element.
